title: Resignations Can Become Contagious
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Turnover is treated here as a social contagion, and the piece is essentially a script for what a leader should say while it is spreading. The mechanism is stated as a piece of reasoning team members run themselves: if someone I respect has concluded it is time to leave, perhaps I should examine the same question. The author notes this happens even on teams with good morale, which decouples the phenomenon from any underlying grievance. The prescribed response begins with an honest assessment for a genuine cause, and, absent one, a posture of unpanicked confidence — protecting the team without sounding an alarm that would confirm the doubt. The most useful part of the argument is its list of errors: apologising for departures, or voicing regret that valued colleagues have left, both read as confirmation that something is wrong and invite further questions. The alternative is to keep private lament private, direct attention and recognition toward the best remaining performers, and frame vacancies as chances to hire better. The closing turn argues that this forward-looking confidence is not crisis messaging but the right message at all times.
points: The contagion is explained as inference rather than mood: a respected colleague's exit functions as evidence, prompting others to reassess their own trajectory.
The author insists the effect appears even in high-morale teams, which is why treating every resignation wave as a symptom of a real problem misreads it.
The two named errors are apologising for departures and expressing regret about them — both undermine team confidence by validating the doubt others are already entertaining.
The recommended redirection is specific: attention and recognition toward top performers, and vacancies framed as openings to bring in even better talent.
The memorable image is that the best team members are too busy growing their own lush grass to go looking for greener grass elsewhere.
quotes: Once a trusted and valued colleague departs for greener grass somewhere else, it encourages others to evaluate their own career trajectories.
Even in teams with great morale, once one team member departs, it is not uncommon to see others follow them out the door.
A common error leaders make is to apologize for the fact people are departing.
Both apologies and regrets undermine team confidence and encourage more questions and doubts.
They focus their attention and recognition on their best performers and remind everyone of the need to replace departing colleagues with even better talent.
Inwardly they know that the best team members are far too busy growing their own lush grass to look for greener grass elsewhere.
